## 2024 Ballot, Damages, and the Border Deal (January 2024)

In late January 2024 Trump was simultaneously the presumptive Republican presidential nominee and the target of multiple legal actions. He publicly attacked the bipartisan Senate border-and-Ukraine package then under negotiation, characterizing the compromise as a political "gift" to Democrats, and his opposition was widely credited with helping to collapse Republican support for the deal.[[N]] House Speaker [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] echoed that resistance, suggesting the compromise would be "dead on arrival" in his chamber.[[N]]

On the legal front, the U.S. Supreme Court signaled that it was moving rapidly on Trump's appeal seeking to overturn the [[colorado-supreme-court|Colorado Supreme Court]] ruling that barred him from the state's ballot on Fourteenth Amendment grounds, scheduling oral argument for February 8, 2024 and indicating that written opinions would be announced the same day.[[N]] His attorneys' January 3 petition asked whether the Colorado court had incorrectly ordered him excluded from the 2024 presidential ballot.[[N]] Days earlier, a New York jury ordered Trump to pay $83.3 million in the second [[e-jean-carroll|E. Jean Carroll]] defamation case; he denounced the verdict on Truth Social as "absolutely ridiculous" and described the legal system as "out of control."[[N]]

Badlands writer [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] framed these proceedings through the phrase "Trump is the President of Precedent," arguing that each legal and narrative deployment against Trump was building the record for a broader confrontation, and that "they're not after him, they're after you — he's just in the way."[[N]]

## Snoop Dogg Reversal (January 2024)

The rapper [[snoop-dogg|Snoop Dogg]] said in a January 28, 2024 interview with The Times that he had "nothing but love and respect" for Trump, citing Trump's pardon of Michael Harris, co-founder of Snoop's first label Death Row Records.[[N]] Badlands writer [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] contrasted this with Snoop's 2017 "Lavender" video, in which he aimed a gun at a clown dressed as Trump, and argued that Trump-era policies such as the First Step Act, Opportunity Zones and the Platinum Plan had been misrepresented by the corporate press.[[N]]

## Border Bill Push and the Jordan Drone Attack (January 2024)

On Friday, January 26, 2024, Biden publicly pressed [[congress|Congress]] to embrace a bipartisan Senate deal pairing border enforcement measures with Ukraine aid, saying in a statement that the proposed policies would "be the toughest and fairest set of reforms to secure the border we've ever had in our country."[[N]] He pledged to use a new emergency authority to "shut down the border" as soon as he could sign the measure into law.[[N]] Senate Republicans had initially insisted that border policy changes be attached to Biden's $110 billion emergency request covering Ukraine, Israel, immigration enforcement and other national security needs, but the deal came under heavy Republican fire and House Speaker [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] suggested it was "dead on arrival."[[N]] Johnson wrote that "rather than accept accountability, President Biden is now trying to blame Congress for what HE himself intentionally created."[[N]]

Badlands writer [[chris-paul|Chris Paul]] argued that no legislation was needed at all, contending the border problem could be solved with existing executive authority and that the bill's real function was to expand the surveillance state while making illegal entry more efficient — a position summarized as "No deals on the border. No deals for foreign proxy 'wars.'"[[N]]

Biden also won the New Hampshire Democratic primary as a write-in candidate that week.[[N]] On Sunday, January 28, after three U.S. Army soldiers were killed and more than thirty service members injured in a drone strike on Tower 22 in northeast Jordan, Biden said while speaking in South Carolina, "We shall respond."[[N]] [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] argued that on a narrative level the episode left Biden appearing "feckless and weak on the world stage."[[N]]

## Opposition to the 2024 Border-Ukraine Deal

In late January 2024, as House Speaker, Johnson responded to President [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]]'s call for [[congress|Congress]] to pass a bipartisan Senate border-and-Ukraine package by suggesting the compromise on border and immigration policy could be "dead on arrival" in his chamber.[[N]] In a letter addressing the negotiations he wrote that "rather than accept accountability, President Biden is now trying to blame Congress for what HE himself intentionally created."[[N]] Johnson's resistance, alongside public opposition from [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], contributed to the collapse of Senate Republican support for the deal, with potentially far-reaching consequences for U.S. allies — Ukraine in particular — that depended on the attached $110 billion emergency funding request.[[N]]

## The 2024 Border-Ukraine Supplemental Fight

In January 2024 Congress was the arena for a bipartisan Senate effort to pair border enforcement measures with Ukraine aid inside President [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]]'s $110 billion emergency funding request covering Ukraine, Israel, immigration enforcement and other national security needs.[[N]] Senate Republicans had initially demanded that border policy changes be attached to the request, but the emerging deal came under fire from Republicans including [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], who called it a political "gift" to Democrats, and House Speaker [[mike-johnson|Mike Johnson]] indicated it could be "dead on arrival" in the House.[[N]] Reporting at the time noted that the diminishing prospects for passage carried far-reaching consequences for U.S. allies abroad, especially Ukraine, and that Biden's embrace of the deal amid Republican resistance could mark an election-year shift in the politics of immigration.[[N]] Badlands commentary from [[chris-paul|Chris Paul]] argued that Congress needed to pass no legislation whatsoever, since the executive already possessed full authority to secure the border, and characterized both parties' pursuit of a deal as [[uniparty|Uniparty]] behavior.[[N]]

## Texas Spending (2023–2024)

State campaign finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital and reported in January 2024 showed Soros pouring extensive sums into Texas in an attempt to flip the traditionally Republican state to Democrats.[[N]] Over the preceding year he contributed more than $3 million to at least five left-wing groups in the state to build political infrastructure and help Democrats make gains.[[N]] Among the recipients was Texas Majority PAC, an under-the-radar group positioning itself to turn the state blue, which Fox News Digital had reported in August 2023 received hundreds of thousands of dollars from Soros' Democracy PAC II; the financier was described as single-handedly propelling that organization.[[N]]

Badlands writer [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] used the story to revisit claims that Soros has been "banned" from multiple countries, noting fact-checkers' distinction that it was the [[open-society-foundations|Open Society Foundations]] rather than Soros personally that ceased operations in Hungary in 2018 after passage of the so-called "Stop Soros" law targeting its work with illegal immigrants.[[N]] She argued the Hungarian precedent was directly relevant because Soros holds dual U.S. and Hungarian citizenship and because the banned Hungarian activities concerned immigration, much like the Texas spending — with the difference being the degree of influence his money buys over American decision-makers.[[N]]

## Hungary Precedent and the Texas Comparison (2024)

In January 2024 Badlands commentary revisited the Open Society Foundations' 2018 withdrawal from Hungary, noting that OSF said it was forced to shutter operations there after the government passed the "Stop Soros" law, which outlawed much of the group's work with illegal immigrants in the country.[[N]] Fact-checking outlets had cited this history while disputing claims that [[george-soros|George Soros]] himself had been banned from six countries, resting the rebuttal on the distinction between the man and his charities.[[N]] Badlands writer [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] argued the distinction was thin and that the Hungarian episode illuminated OSF-aligned spending in Texas, where more than $3 million flowed to left-wing groups seeking to flip the state.[[N]]

## New Hampshire Ballot Access (January 2024)

On the same day President [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] learned he had won the New Hampshire Democratic primary as a write-in candidate, Kennedy — running as an independent presidential candidate — announced that his campaign had gathered the required number of signatures to appear on the state's general election ballot in November 2024.[[N]] His team collected more than 3,000 signatures in a single day in the Granite State, according to a campaign statement.[[N]] Kennedy thanked "our dedicated supporters and volunteers," adding that "democracy is much more than voting" and that the enthusiasm for collecting signatures, creating new political parties and rallying for change would "get us onto the ballot in every state and fuel our voter registration and GOTV operation."[[N]]

Badlands writer [[simon-esler|Simon Esler]] treated the milestone as evidence that Kennedy was becoming a live possibility in 2024, arguing that voters were weary of engineered political polarization.[[N]] While crediting [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] with a deeper awareness of the information war — grounded in the Q drops and the [[devolution|Devolution]] research — Esler argued that Kennedy embodies a distinct asset: family legacy, historically an Achilles heel for the [[deep-state|Deep State]].[[N]] He contrasted the Kennedy line with the Bush, Rockefeller and Rothschild legacies, which he described as multigenerational vehicles for war propaganda, the United Nations and Agenda 2030, and centuries of banking power respectively, concluding that a victory by an "America First family legacy" — whether as president or as Trump's running mate — would carry major symbolic weight.[[N]]

## Peace-Talk Reports and Kremlin Denial (January 2024)

In late January 2024, as the war in Ukraine approached its two-year mark, international press chatter grew that Moscow was seeking a deal to end the conflict.[[N]] The New York Times had reported in December 2023 that Putin was "quietly signaling" to the West that he wanted a ceasefire, and Bloomberg revived the storyline on January 25, 2024, citing two anonymous sources close to the Kremlin who said Putin's officials had used diplomatic back-channels to "put out feelers" to senior Biden administration officials in December.[[N]] The [[kremlin|Kremlin]] issued a firm denial that Friday, with spokesman [[dmitry-peskov|Dmitry Peskov]] telling a press briefing of the Bloomberg article, "That's false information, it's completely untrue."[[N]]

Badlands writer [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]] read the reporting as narrative reframing by the "Media Industrial Complex," arguing that Putin was not begging Western bureaucrats for peace and that Russia had demonstrated durability against sanctions and pressure; in his framing, "retreat is defeat in the Mind War," and the Establishment was ceding previously held narrative ground.[[N]]
entities/dmitry-peskov.md:
## Denial of Ukraine Peace-Feeler Reports (January 2024)

On Friday, January 26, 2024, Peskov responded to a Bloomberg report claiming that officials working for [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] had used diplomatic back-channels in December to "put out feelers" to senior Biden administration officials about ending the war in Ukraine.[[N]] Speaking at a press briefing, Peskov said of the report: "That's false information, it's completely untrue."[[N]] The denial, issued on behalf of the [[kremlin|Kremlin]], also implicitly rejected earlier New York Times reporting from December 2023 that Putin was "quietly signaling" a desire for a ceasefire.[[N]]

## Quiet Electoral Reform Push (January 2024)

In January 2024 CTV News reported that teams working for Trudeau and NDP leader Jagmeet Singh had quietly been in talks to table electoral reform legislation before the next federal vote, as part of the Liberal-NDP confidence-and-supply agreement.[[N]] Public Safety, Democratic Institutions and Intergovernmental Affairs Minister Dominic LeBlanc led the negotiations for the government, with NDP MP and democratic reform critic Daniel Blaikie for his party; Blaikie said "a fair amount of work" had been done toward drafting amendments to the Canada Elections Act.[[N]] The package fell short of the full overhaul of the federal voting system Trudeau had once promised, instead bundling proposals aimed at expanding "the ability for people to vote."[[N]]

Badlands writer [[simon-esler|Simon Esler]] situated the move within a difficult week for Trudeau: within a seven-day span a world-class MMA fighter attacked his character, Canada's highest court ruled his use of the [[emergencies-act|Emergencies Act]] during the Freedom Convoy unlawful, and Tucker Carlson launched a "Liberate Canada" campaign against his platform.[[N]] Esler highlighted three headline proposals — an expanded three-day voting period during general elections, allowing voters to cast ballots at any polling place within their riding, and changes to the mail-in ballot process — and argued they resembled the "copy-paste" election-administration changes the globalist establishment had used elsewhere, calling them "the moves of someone scared to lose power."[[N]]

## Expedited Handling of Trump v. Anderson (January 2024)

In late January 2024 the Supreme Court signaled that it was moving quickly on former President [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]]'s appeal seeking to overturn the [[colorado-supreme-court|Colorado Supreme Court]] ruling that barred him from the state's ballot on [[fourteenth-amendment|Fourteenth Amendment]] grounds.[[N]] A note accompanying the Court's schedule for February 8 — the day set for the first oral arguments in the case — indicated that the Court intended to announce written opinions on the very same day.[[N]] While the substance of those opinions was not revealed, observers read the announcement as a signal that the justices regarded the case as having significant legal importance warranting expedited consideration.[[N]] The question presented in Trump's attorneys' January 3 petition was whether the Colorado Supreme Court had incorrectly ordered him excluded from the 2024 presidential ballot.[[N]]
entities/colorado-supreme-court.md:
## Appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court (January 2024)

The Colorado Supreme Court's ruling barring [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] from the state's presidential ballot on [[fourteenth-amendment|Fourteenth Amendment]] grounds was appealed to the [[supreme-court-of-the-united-states|U.S. Supreme Court]], which by late January 2024 had signaled it was moving quickly on the case.[[N]] Trump's attorneys filed their petition on January 3, 2024, presenting the question of whether the Colorado court incorrectly ordered him excluded from the 2024 presidential ballot; oral argument was set for February 8, with written opinions expected the same day.[[N]]

## $83.3 Million Defamation Verdict (January 2024)

In late January 2024 a jury ordered former President [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] to pay $83.3 million in Carroll's second civil defamation trial.[[N]] Carroll had accused Trump of sexually assaulting her in the mid-1990s in a dressing room at the Bergdorf Goodman department store in Manhattan; although the alleged attack occurred decades earlier, she sued under New York's Adult Survivors Act, which allows victims to bring civil damages claims beyond the ordinary statute of limitations.[[N]] Trump responded on Truth Social, calling the award "absolutely ridiculous" and raging that the legal system was "out of control."[[N]]

## Georgia Senate Investigative Panel (January 2024)

On Friday, January 26, 2024, the Republican-led Georgia Senate approved a resolution establishing a special committee to investigate Willis, the Fulton County District Attorney who had brought an election interference case against [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] and eighteen co-defendants the previous year.[[N]] The 30-19 vote fell along party lines.[[N]] The resolution cited misconduct allegations that "include the ongoing expenditure of significant public funds for the purpose of hiring a special assistant district attorney with whom District Attorney Willis had, and may yet have, an ongoing romantic relationship."[[N]] Under the resolution the panel would consist of no more than nine members, including at least three Democrats.[[N]]

## Tower 22 Drone Attack (January 2024)

U.S. Central Command confirmed in a statement on Sunday, January 28, 2024 that three service members were killed and at least 34 injured in a one-way drone attack that "impacted at a base in northeast Jordan."[[N]] Eight injured service members were medically evacuated for higher-level care, CENTCOM said, and officials expected the number of wounded to rise as personnel sought treatment for symptoms consistent with traumatic brain injury.[[N]] The strike on the outpost known as Tower 22, near the Syrian border, marked the first time U.S. troops had been killed by enemy fire in the Middle East since the start of the Gaza war; officials said the drone was fired by Iran-backed militants and appeared to come from Syria, though the specific militia responsible remained undetermined.[[N]]

## Commentary: No Deals on the Border (January 2024)

Writing in the Badlands News Brief in late January 2024, Paul rejected the bipartisan Senate border-and-Ukraine package outright, arguing that "the border problem could be solved without any legislation whatsoever."[[N]] In his reading, the legislation was not designed to solve the border crisis but "to increase the surveillance state while making the process of illegal alien entry more efficient," with an added $110 billion committed to what he called "fake foreign proxy wars."[[N]] His prescription was a flat refusal — "No deals. No deals on the border. No deals for foreign proxy 'wars.'" — on the grounds that full authority to solve the problem already exists and the crisis persists because both sides of the [[uniparty|Uniparty]] want it to.[[N]] He asked why Republican representatives were discussing new legislation rather than demanding the executive use the authorities the people had already transferred to the State.[[N]]

## Commentary in Badlands News Brief 169 (January 2024)

Burning Bright contributed several analyses to the January 29, 2024 brief. On the border debate he offered a first-principles argument that "sovereignty radiates from the ground up," describing as "the greatest PsyOp in human history" the notion that sovereignty is bestowed top-down; in his framing it begins within each man and projects outward through family, town, city, state and nation, making the America First movement the opposite of a merely national movement.[[N]]

On the Tower 22 drone attack in Jordan he described the news as evidence that "the Shadow War is still alive and well" and that the enemy retained kinetic power projection through proxies, urging readers to embrace the "Understanding > Reacting" refrain while noting that narratively [[joe-biden|Joe Biden]] appeared feckless and weak.[[N]]

On reports that [[vladimir-putin|Vladimir Putin]] was seeking peace talks, he argued the coverage was narrative reframing by the Media Industrial Complex and that "retreat is defeat in the Mind War."[[N]] On the $83.3 million [[e-jean-carroll|Carroll]] verdict and the ballot disqualification case he advanced the formulation that [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]] is "the President of Precedent," arguing that the campaign against Trump was ultimately aimed at the public — "They're not after him. They're after you. He's just in the way" — and closing with "Think Mirror, and be comfy."[[N]]

## Commentary in Badlands News Brief 169 (January 2024)

Ashe in America wrote two items for the January 29, 2024 brief. On [[george-soros|George Soros]]' Texas spending she disputed the framing of the financier as a benevolent philanthropist, citing fact-checking coverage of the [[open-society-foundations|Open Society Foundations]]' 2018 exit from Hungary under the "Stop Soros" law and arguing that the distinction between the man and his charities was a thin rebuttal, particularly given his dual U.S.-Hungarian citizenship and the immigration focus of both the Hungarian and Texas operations.[[N]]

On [[snoop-dogg|Snoop Dogg]]'s newly expressed "love and respect" for [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], she recalled the rapper's 2017 "Lavender" video alongside Madonna's remarks about blowing up the White House and Kathy Griffin's severed-head photo shoot, noting that all three were lawfully protected First Amendment expression and that no one in MAGA had sought to strip those creators of their rights — a contrast she used against claims that "peacefully and patriotically" is a violent dog whistle.[[N]] She argued that the corporate press had successfully painted MAGA as a return to Jim Crow while ignoring Trump-era measures aimed at Black Americans, including the First Step Act, Opportunity Zones and the Platinum Plan, and welcomed Snoop's defection from the media narrative.[[N]]

## News Brief 169: "Battle Lines Drawn in All Theaters" (January 29, 2024)

The January 29, 2024 edition of the Badlands News Brief surveyed the weekend's news across domestic and foreign theaters: the collapsing Senate border-and-Ukraine deal, [[george-soros|George Soros]]' spending in Texas, [[robert-f-kennedy-jr|Robert F. Kennedy Jr.]]'s New Hampshire ballot access, the Tower 22 drone attack in Jordan, [[snoop-dogg|Snoop Dogg]]'s reversal on [[donald-trump|Donald Trump]], the [[kremlin|Kremlin]]'s denial of peace-talk reports, Canadian electoral reform, the expedited Supreme Court ballot case, the $83.3 million [[e-jean-carroll|Carroll]] verdict, and a bonus item on the Georgia Senate panel to investigate [[fani-willis|Fani Willis]].[[N]] Commentary came from [[chris-paul|Chris Paul]], [[burning-bright|Burning Bright]], [[ashe-in-america|Ashe in America]] and [[simon-esler|Simon Esler]], reflecting the brief's standard format of hand-picked items paired with original, explicitly subjective takes.[[N]]
